archetype.name: Retooling (offense ahead of defense)
archetype.definition: A team with a functional, careful offense around Jayden Daniels, two years removed from a 12-win season, whose defense has been bottom-tier for a second straight year and keeps the record buried.

report.headline: A league-average offense chained to the league's worst scoring defense.
report.take:
Washington is not the 12-win, fourth-ranked offense of 2024, and it isn't the collapse of 2025 either. The offense sits right at the league median: 17th in EPA per play, mid-pack in points and yards, with Daniels starting five of six games. The problem is the other side. The defense ranks 25th in EPA allowed and has given up 172 points, the most in football by points allowed per game. After ranking 31st in 2025, this looks like a continuation, not a rough patch.

The defense is lopsided. Against the run it is genuinely good: 6th in rush EPA allowed and 2nd in explosive-run rate allowed. Against the pass it breaks: 27th in pass EPA allowed, 23rd on deep throws, 32nd against opposing tight ends, and teams know it. Opponents pass on Washington at the third-highest rate over normal in the league. Seattle, a bottom-ten offense today, threw for 393 yards on them. The pass rush gets home often (6th in pressure rate) but finishes rarely (9 sacks, 26th). In the red zone, opponents have scored touchdowns on 83.3% of trips, dead last.

The raw record hides how much has already gone right. Washington has turned it over just twice in six games and is +6 in turnover margin, 3rd in the league per game. Usually that buys wins, but it bought one and a tie. The point differential implies about 1.8 wins, so this is not an unlucky team. Special teams are a hidden leak, 29th in EPA per game. Some things should improve: red-zone touchdown rates this extreme rarely hold, and a top-ten pressure rate should turn into more sacks. But the giveaway rate will drift back toward normal, and when it does the margin for error shrinks further.

The outlook is better than 1-4-1 sounds because of context. The NFC East leader is 3-2-1, Philadelphia has lost Jalen Hurts for the season, and seven of the ten games after this week come against teams that currently have losing records. Against that, Terry McLaurin is out, lead back Jacory Croskey-Merritt is on IR, and the backup quarterback is hurt. This is a team that can climb back toward the middle of the pack, but only if the pass defense stops handing out explosive plays.

strengths.title: Elite ball security so far
strengths.body: Two giveaways in six games is the main reason a mediocre team hasn't been blown out more often. Daniels has kept the ball out of harm's way, and the defense has added takeaways at a league-average clip. Expect some regression; nobody sustains this rate over a full season. Still, it reflects a quarterback who isn't forcing throws.

strengths.title: A run defense that holds
strengths.body: Washington is 6th in rush EPA allowed and rarely gives up a long run, which keeps early downs manageable. The flip side is that offenses simply stop running and attack the weaker pass defense. Still, it is a real, schematic strength, and it travels well against run-dependent offenses.

strengths.title: Line creates room up front
strengths.body: Backs average 3.38 yards before contact, 3rd in the league, so the run blocking is doing its job. The run game still ranks only 21st in EPA, which means the backs are getting less out of good blocking than they should. The 202-yard day against the Giants shows what happens when the two line up. With Croskey-Merritt on IR, Rachaad White inherits good blocking.

concerns.title: Pass defense is the whole problem
concerns.body: Opponents throw on Washington far more than normal because it works. The defense is 27th in pass EPA allowed, gets beaten deep, and has been shredded by tight ends. This repeats the 2025 defense, so it looks structural rather than a slump. Short-area coverage is solid; the damage comes over the top and down the seam.

concerns.title: Losing with every break going right
concerns.body: Washington is +6 in turnovers and still 1-4-1, and the point differential says that record is about fair. Turnover margins drift toward zero, and special teams ranked 29th give back field position every week. The red-zone defense should improve from historically bad, but that only offsets the turnover regression.

concerns.title: Thin roster, leaky protection
concerns.body: The line allows pressure at the 29th-ranked rate, partly because Daniels holds the ball (7th-longest time to throw). Now McLaurin is out, Croskey-Merritt is on IR, and backup Marcus Mariota is hurt. That matters: Mariota's lone start was a 13-30 loss with a pass EPA of -9.5. A Daniels injury would expose how little depth there is.

trend.note: Results have swung from a 33-31 win over Seattle to 17-point losses to Dallas and Indianapolis. With Daniels starting, though, the games have mostly been competitive, including a cover at San Francisco. The worst result came in the one Mariota start.

nextGame.headline: Hurts-less Eagles bring a soft run defense and no pass rush
nextGame.body:
Washington comes off a bye with 13 days of rest to host an Eagles team that has fallen apart. Philadelphia ranks 30th in net EPA and 28th on offense, can't stop the run (30th in rush EPA allowed), barely pressures the quarterback (27th in pressure rate, last in QB hit rate), and misses tackles at the 31st-ranked rate. Washington's offense has been average, and against this defense average may be enough. The Book had not posted a line at the time of the dossier. In Week 1, Washington ran for 132 yards and lost 24-22 in Philadelphia, but that was with Hurts.

Availability favors Washington on paper. Hurts is out for the season with blood clots, so Tanner McKee starts, and right tackle Lane Johnson is out. Landon Dickerson, Saquon Barkley and several defenders carried return estimates around Week 7, so check their status. The Eagles' top two tight ends are on IR, which shields Washington's worst coverage matchup. On Washington's side, McLaurin is out, Croskey-Merritt is on IR, Mariota won't back up Daniels, Charles Omenihu is out, and Javon Kinlaw is questionable, which thins a rush that needs to finish plays against McKee.

waysToWin.title: Run behind the line all day
waysToWin.body: Washington's blockers create the third-most room before contact in the league. Philadelphia's run defense is 30th in EPA allowed and misses tackles constantly. Even without Croskey-Merritt, White and Daniels' legs should find steady gains and help the offense control the clock.

waysToWin.title: Feed Diggs against weak WR1 coverage
waysToWin.body: With McLaurin out, Stefon Diggs, already the target leader, becomes the clear No. 1. Philadelphia has been among the worst in the league at covering opposing top receivers. A weak Eagles pass rush also gives Daniels the extra beat he likes to hold the ball.

waysToWin.title: Make McKee win from behind
waysToWin.body: Philadelphia's offense was 28th in EPA even with Hurts and runs poorly (27th in run EPA). That plays right into Washington's strong run defense. An early lead forces a backup quarterback, missing Lane Johnson, to throw into Washington's top-ten pressure rate.

waysToLose.title: Busted coverage makes McKee look good
waysToLose.body: Washington has turned bottom-tier passing offenses into big days, Seattle's 393 yards included. If the rush keeps arriving without finishing, McKee gets enough clean deep shots to steal the game.

waysToLose.title: Losing the hidden-yardage battle
waysToLose.body: Philadelphia is 6th in special-teams EPA per game; Washington is 29th. Philadelphia also goes for it on fourth down more aggressively than anyone. In a low-scoring, field-position game, those edges can decide it.

waysToLose.title: Red-zone defense gives up sevens
waysToLose.body: Opponents have scored touchdowns on 83.3% of red-zone trips, the worst rate in the league. Even a limited Eagles offense can win if its few trips inside the 20 all end in touchdowns.

nextGame.watch: Whether Washington's pass rush, top-ten at getting pressure but bottom-ten at sacks, finally finishes against a backup quarterback playing without Lane Johnson.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense should hold roughly where it is, an average unit that protects the ball. It will give the ball away more often than twice per six games, and losing McLaurin for now and Croskey-Merritt into late November lowers its ceiling. The defense is the swing. The 83.3% red-zone touchdown rate and the gap between pressures and sacks should both drift toward normal, which would shave points off the league-worst scoring defense. The coverage problems look structural, though; they mirror 2025. Expect a team that plays closer to average than its record without becoming a good one.

The schedule and division are the reasons to stay interested. Six of the remaining ten opponents are currently 2-4 or worse, the division leader is 3-2-1, and Philadelphia has lost its quarterback. A realistic path is a run into the six- or seven-win range, with only a remote shot at contention unless the pass defense changes. If turnover luck turns and the defense doesn't improve, four or five wins is just as plausible.
swingFactors: Pass defense improvement, especially deep and against tight ends
Daniels staying healthy with no healthy backup

confidence.note: Six games, one start by the backup QB, and key injuries on offense; the defensive pattern matches last season.
